explain.say: Inside a thunderstorm, strong updrafts toss ice crystals and soft hail pellets, called graupel, against each other. Each collision passes tiny electric charges between them.

faq.a: In a thunderstorm, ice crystals and soft hail collide in strong updrafts and swap tiny electric charges. Light positive crystals rise to the top and heavier negative pellets gather lower down.
asks: What causes the charge in a storm cloud?

faq.a: A huge current heats a narrow channel of air to about 30,000 degrees Celsius in a split second. Air that hot glows brilliantly white.

faq.q: Does lightning go up or down?
faq.a: Both. A faint leader comes down from the cloud first, then the bright return stroke we see races upward from the ground along the same path.

faq.q: Does lightning strike the same place twice?
faq.a: Yes, often. Tall, pointed objects are struck again and again; the Empire State Building is hit about 20 times a year.
asks: Can lightning hit the same spot twice?

faq.q: How do I stay safe in a thunderstorm?
faq.a: Go indoors or into a hard-topped car, and stay away from open fields, water and lone trees. If you can hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck.

facts: Lightning flashes about 44 times every second around the world, about 1.4 billion flashes a year.
About three quarters of lightning flashes stay inside or between clouds and never reach the ground.

quiz.say: In a typical thunderstorm cloud, where does most of the negative charge gather?
quiz.show: Negative charge in a storm cloud gathers mostly…
quiz.why: Heavier graupel pellets pick up negative charge and stay lower in the cloud, while light positive ice crystals are carried to the top.

wrong.0: The top of the cloud mostly collects light, positively charged ice crystals.
wrong.2: The charges build up inside the cloud, where the ice collides.
